question.:question/problem: A heated metal body cools in a room at ${24}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Its temperature is ${97}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $1$ minute and ${75}^{∘}\text{C}$ after $4$ minutes. The temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Celsius, obeys Newton's law of cooling, with $t$ measured in minutes since cooling began. To the nearest minute, how long after cooling began does the body reach ${30}^{∘}\text{C}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-24),\qquad k>0.
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-24| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-24>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-24 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-24 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-24 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =24+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

Apply the two observed conditions $T(1)=97$ and $T(4)=75$:

$$
\begin{aligned}97 & =24+Ke^{-1k} \\ 73 & =Ke^{-1k} \\ 75 & =24+Ke^{-4k} \\ 51 & =Ke^{-4k}\end{aligned}
$$

Divide the excess temperatures to eliminate $K$, then take natural logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{51}{73} & =\frac{Ke^{-4k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{51}{73} & =e^{-3k} \\ \ln(\frac{51}{73}) & =-3k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=97$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}73 & =Ke^{-1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3})} \\ K & =73e^{1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3})} \\ K & =73\left(\frac{73}{51}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution satisfying both observations is

$$
T(t)=24+73\left(\frac{73}{51}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3})t}.
$$

Substituting the two observation times confirms the model:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =24+(73\left(\frac{73}{51}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}})e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3})\cdot 1}=97 \\ T(4) & =24+(73\left(\frac{73}{51}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}})e^{-(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3})\cdot 4}=75\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the body reaches ${30}^{∘}\text{C}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =30 \\ 24+Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =30 \\ Ke^{-k{t}_{1}} & =6 \\ e^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{6}{K} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\ln\left(\frac{6}{K}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{6}{K}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the values of $K$ and $k$ to obtain the time measured since cooling began:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{51}{73} \right)}}{3}}\ln\left(\frac{6}{73\left(\frac{73}{51}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}}\right) \\ {t}_{1} & =1+3\frac{\ln(\frac{6}{73})}{\ln(\frac{51}{73})}≈22\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$
